name: Ute Agreement of March 6, 1880, ratified by the Act of June 15, 1880 (Ute removal from Colorado)
aka: Agreement with the Confederated Bands of Utes, 1880
nations: Núuchi-u (Ute): White River, Uncompahgre (Tabeguache) and Southern (Muache, Capote, Weeminuche) bands
promises: The Ute bands would cede the whole of their Colorado reservation, except land for the bands' settlement, to the United States.

The Uncompahgre were to settle on agricultural land on the Grand River in Colorado if enough could be found, or in Utah; the White River Utes on the Uintah reservation in Utah; the Southern Utes on the La Plata River.
The ceded land was to be sold and the proceeds, after costs, held in trust for the Utes, with annuities and allotments in severalty.

breaches.what: In the Supreme Court the United States admitted that the stated consideration for the 1880 cession was not promptly paid. The Court also recorded that the claims arising from the cession were settled by Court of Claims consent judgments in 1950 exceeding $31 million in aggregate.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States, Brief for Petitioner, as recorded in United States v. Southern Ute Tribe or Band of Indians, 402 U.S. 159 (1971), note 3

source.title: United States v. Southern Ute Tribe or Band of Indians, 402 U.S. 159 (1971)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

breaches.quote: The United States admits that the stated consideration was not promptly paid.

breaches.what: The Supreme Court described the Act of June 15, 1880 as Congress, aroused by the 1879 White River killings, taking steps to punish the Indians involved, to dispossess the Utes of their reservation and to remove them from Colorado. The White River and Uncompahgre Utes left for Utah before 1882.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Confederated Bands of Ute Indians v. United States, 330 U.S. 169 (1947); United States v. Southern Ute Tribe, 402 U.S. 159 (1971)

breaches.what: The Uncompahgre Band claimed that the United States failed to give it the reservation the 1880 agreement required, in Colorado or Utah. The claim was settled for $300,000 without a finding on the merits.

breaches.what: The Southern Ute Tribe claimed the United States breached its duty under the 1880 and 1895 Acts by giving away 220,000 acres as free homesteads instead of selling them for the tribe, and by failing to account for proceeds of 82,000 acres. The Supreme Court held the claim barred by the 1950 consent judgments, without deciding its merits.

breaches.what: The Ute Indian Tribe states that its people were forced out of Colorado at gunpoint on a march in which ancestors died, and that the Uncompahgre Reservation homelands should be restored to the Tribe.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Ute Business Committee and Chairman Shaun Chapoose, statement on the Camp Hale-Continental Divide National Monument, October 12, 2022, as reported by the Deseret News

source.title: Utah's Ute Indian Tribe blasts Biden's Colorado national monument

breaches.quote: the forced death march at the hands of the United States as we were moved out of Colorado at gunpoint

landTaken: The Supreme Court (1971) describes the Ute reservation as approximately 15.7 million acres before the 1874 Brunot Cession of 3.7 million acres; the 1880 Act ceded the rest except the lands reserved for settlement, after which only the Southern Utes remained in Colorado.
compensation: Court of Claims consent judgments in 1950 (Confederated Bands of Ute Indians v. United States, 117 Ct. Cl. 433) exceeding $31 million in aggregate for lands ceded under the 1880 Act; $300,000 to the Uncompahgre Band (ICC Docket 349, 1965).
today: The White River and Uncompahgre Utes live on the Uintah and Ouray Reservation in Utah; the Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute reservations remain in Colorado.

nationVoice.nation: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
nationVoice.summary: The Ute Business Committee, in an October 2022 statement, said its ancestors were marched out of Colorado at gunpoint by the United States, that the Tribe still holds treaty rights in those homelands, and that the President must restore and secure the Uncompahgre Reservation homelands.

openQuestions: The agreement's own text (Kappler, vol. 1, p. 180, or 21 Stat. 199) was not opened; the promises above are summarized from the Supreme Court's 1947 and 1971 descriptions and the Indian Claims Commission's 1965 and 1966 decisions, and should be checked against the statute.
The 1880 agreement's March 6 date is Royce's; the Act ratifying it is dated June 15, 1880. The 'ratified' field holds the Act's date.
The 1950 consent judgments (117 Ct. Cl. 433) were settlements; they are recorded as compensation, not as a finding of breach.

Audit 2026-11-08: dropped the line saying no Ute account was found, since the Ute Indian Tribe's 2022 statement is recorded; an account from the Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute tribes is still to be sought.

plain.promised: In return for ceding most of their Colorado reservation, the Ute bands were to get land to settle on, and the ceded land was to be sold with the proceeds held in trust for them.
plain.happened: The United States admitted to the Supreme Court that the price was not promptly paid. The Court described the 1880 Act as Congress moving to dispossess the Utes and remove them from Colorado; the White River and Uncompahgre Utes left for Utah.
plain.today: Consent judgments in 1950 exceeded $31 million, and the Uncompahgre Band settled a claim for $300,000 in 1965. The Ute Indian Tribe asks that its Uncompahgre Reservation homelands be restored.
